works.title: Santoro et al 2016
works.why: Listed as a source on implicit meta-learning emerging from training on many related tasks.

works.title: Wang et al 2018
works.why: DeepMind's meta-reinforcement-learning work, discussed as the source of Botvinick's observation that meta-learning emerges unavoidably.

works.title: Botvinick et al 2019a
works.why: Listed as a source on implicit meta-learning emerging in reinforcement learning systems.

works.title: Clune 2019
works.why: Listed as further reading on emergent meta-learning supporting the blessings-of-scale argument.

works.title: Schmidhuber 2015/2018
works.why: Listed as further reading on meta-learning, tying the scaling hypothesis to earlier connectionist ideas Schmidhuber championed.

works.title: Weng 2018/Weng 2019
works.why: Listed as further reading surveys on meta-learning.

works.title: Jukebox
works.why: OpenAI's raw-audio music model, cited as another example of scaling producing surprising new capabilities just before GPT-3.

works.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
works.why: Opens the 'Flexing GPT' section with an epigraph about reason being unfair, framing GPT-3's startling plainness of method.

works.title: Hernandez & Brown 2020
works.why: Used to estimate how training costs for a fixed performance level fall over time through algorithmic efficiency gains.

works.title: T5
works.why: Cited as one of several large language models whose scaling suggested performance might be plateauing before GPT-3 arrived.

works.title: EfficientNet
works.why: Cited as an example showing that even basic hyperparameters like network width, if optimized, can meaningfully change performance.

works.title: LeCun 2019
works.why: Source of the 'cake is a lie' framing being pushed back against when arguing GPT-3 is part of the path to general intelligence.

works.title: Banko & Brill 2001
works.why: Cited as an early example of simple statistical methods eventually beating fancier ones once given enough data.

works.title: Brants et al 2007
works.why: Cited alongside other examples of the 'curves cross' effect where neural/statistical methods overtake older approaches with scale.

works.title: Koehn & Knowles 2017
works.why: Cited as another example of data/scale eventually beating older methods in machine translation.

works.title: Thompson et al 2020
works.why: Criticized as an example of poorly controlled scaling-law estimation compared to the dedicated scaling-law papers.

works.title: Turing-NLG
works.why: Cited as the then-largest dense language model, used as a benchmark for whether any competitor has matched GPT-3's scale since.

works.title: MegatronLM
works.why: Listed among large language models whose scaling behavior informed expectations before GPT-3's results arrived.

works.title: CTRL
works.why: Listed among large language models whose scaling behavior informed expectations before GPT-3's results arrived.

works.title: Meena
works.why: Cited both for scaling expectations before GPT-3 and for its perplexity-vs-human-likeness chatbot ratings.

works.title: GPipe
works.why: Listed among large language/training systems whose scaling behavior informed expectations before GPT-3's results arrived.

works.title: WinoGrande
works.why: Used as a benchmark expected to be solved by further scaling, and later cited as a benchmark critics began downplaying once GPT-3 did well.

works.title: AI and Compute
works.why: Supplies the historical compute-growth chart used to compare GPT-3's training cost to past landmark AI systems.

works.title: AlphaGo Zero
works.why: Used as a comparison point for GPT-3's training compute and as an example of scaling simple architectures to superhuman performance.

works.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
works.why: Shows the clean power-law curves relating loss to compute, data and model size that the piece builds its scaling argument on.

works.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
works.why: Is the paper reporting GPT-3's own results, which the whole piece analyzes and extrapolates from.

works.title: Hendrycks et al 2020
works.why: Provides data on how question-answering performance scales with GPT-3 model size.

works.title: Schrimpf et al 2020
works.why: Cited for evidence that language models become more similar to human brain activity as they scale.

works.title: Warstadt et al 2020
works.why: Cited for evidence that language models acquire more human-like linguistic biases as training data grows.

works.title: Child 2020
works.why: Cited as an example of very deep image-generating models (VAEs) catching up to GANs when scaled.

works.title: Vahdat & Kautz 2020
works.why: Cited alongside Child 2020 as evidence deep VAEs match GAN-quality image generation when scaled.

works.title: Dojolonga et al 2020
works.why: Cited for the finding that transfer-learning quality keeps improving with scale even after classification accuracy plateaus.

works.title: Hill et al 2019
works.why: Listed as further reading on emergent generalization from scaled training in agents.

works.title: Chaplot et al 2017
works.why: Listed as further reading on emergent generalization capabilities from scale.

works.title: Yu et al 2018
works.why: Listed as further reading on emergent generalization capabilities from scale.

works.title: Lake 2019
works.why: Listed as further reading on generalization and compositional learning relevant to the blessings-of-scale argument.

works.title: Interactive Agents Group 2020
works.why: Listed as further reading supporting the claim that scale induces generalization in trained agents.

works.title: AlphaZero
works.why: Cited as an example of superhuman performance emerging just from scaling a bigger model with a richer training signal, without hand-built search tricks.

works.title: MuZero
works.why: Cited as evidence that training a network end-to-end on enough data can implicitly learn tree search, surpassing AlphaZero.

works.title: OpenAI Five
works.why: Used repeatedly as an example of a simple architecture stabilizing and improving at massive scale, including minibatches of millions.

works.title: Dactyl
works.why: Cited as an example of a robot-hand control system developing implicit meta-learning after training on millions of randomized environments.

works.title: BigGAN
works.why: Cited as an example of a generative model stabilizing and benefiting from very large minibatches at scale, like OpenAI Five.

works.title: StyleGAN
works.why: Cited as an example of disentangled representations emerging once embeddings are made deep enough.

works.title: Procgen/CoinRun
works.why: Cited as evidence that agents only generalize to unseen levels once trained on thousands of levels rather than hundreds.

works.title: MetaMimic
works.why: Cited as an example of imitation learning generalizing across hundreds of tasks when trained at scale.

works.title: DD-PPO
works.why: Cited as an example of a reinforcement learning system outperforming classical robot planners once scaled by two orders of magnitude.

works.title: ViLBERT/VideoBERT
works.why: Cited as examples of multimodal pretraining producing better representations from fewer data, motivating interest in big multimodal models.

works.title: BiT (Big Transfer)
works.why: Cited as an example of a classifier that transfers and even surpasses human-labeled accuracy on ImageNet at scale.

works.title: ResNeXt
works.why: Cited as another example of a classifier CNN that transfers and robustifies with human-like error patterns at scale.

works.title: Noisy Student
works.why: Cited as another example of a classifier that becomes more robust and human-like in its errors as it scales.

works.title: Orseau et al 2020
works.why: Cited for the idea that a big model encodes countless small sub-models, central to the explanation of why scale helps.

works.title: Viering & Loog 2021
works.why: Cited for the concept of a phase transition in learning, used to explain how a model shifts from memorizing to genuine algorithms.

works.title: The Brain as a Universal Learning Machine
works.why: Cited as an example of the idea that one scalable architecture, like the brain, can handle many different problems uniformly.

works.title: Cambria & White 2014
works.why: Source of the figure depicting hypothetical S-curves of progress in natural language processing research.

works.title: Collobert et al 2011
works.why: Quoted for the estimate of the entropy gap between n-gram models and humans, underlying the 'last bits are deepest' argument.

works.title: Shannon 1951 (entropy of English)
works.why: Provides the classic human-subject estimate of English text entropy used to anchor claims about how much is left for a model to learn.

works.title: Teahan & Cleary 1996
works.why: Gives an n-gram model entropy estimate used for comparison with human and neural-model text prediction performance.

works.title: The Quiet Enemy (from The Legacy of Hiroshima)
works.why: Supplies the anecdote about Bohr doubting an atomic bomb could be built without turning a country into a factory, used as an analogy for scaling skepticism.

works.title: Chelba et al 2013 (One Billion Word Benchmark)
works.why: Source of the 1 Billion Word benchmark used (and critiqued) for comparing human and GPT-2/GPT-3 perplexity.

works.title: The Human Use of Human Beings
works.why: Quoted for the idea that merely knowing a problem has a solution is itself a major clue that accelerates independent discovery, used as an analogy for scaling.

works.title: Ilya Sutskever's public comments on scaling
works.why: Quoted for the view that neural networks plus enough data and compute 'will in fact work,' framing OpenAI's bet on scale.

works.title: Wojciech Zaremba's comments on OpenAI Five (transcript)
works.why: Interview recounting surprise that existing reinforcement learning methods, given enough scale, worked for DoTA2 without needing new algorithms.

works.title: GShard
works.why: Given as an example of a mixture-of-experts model Google Brain works on, contrasted with dense scaled models like GPT-3.

works.title: Agent57
works.why: Cited as an example of DeepMind's 'throw many methods at the wall' approach to incrementally replicating brain modules.

works.title: Hestness et al 2017
works.why: Called an early scaling paper from a Chinese AI company used to argue Chinese AI research also contributed to the scaling literature.

works.title: DynamicEmbedding
works.why: Given as another example of a large but 'shallow' mixture-style model not comparable to dense scaled models like GPT-3.

works.title: Moravec's forecasts of AI hardware progress
works.why: Supplies the decades-old Moore's-law-based prediction that human-level compute cost would become affordable in the 2020s, which the piece says is being…

works.title: Jim Gray's 1999 remarks on neural network hardware
works.why: Quoted as an example of an expert noting hardware existed for brain-scale computation yet assuming it wouldn't produce intelligence, which the piece says was…

works.title: Peter Norvig's account of early neural net experiments
works.why: Interview anecdote illustrating how lack of compute, not ideas, held back neural networks for decades before deep learning's rise.

works.title: Jeff Dean's remarks on the compute slowdown
works.why: Quoted on the irony that general-purpose CPU performance growth is slowing just as machine learning most wants more compute.

works.title: Richard Feynman's Challenger disaster appendix
works.why: Quoted on how prior 'successes' despite warning signs are no guarantee against catastrophe, used as an analogy for dismissing AI risk.

works.title: SayCan
works.why: Cited as evidence that a language model, given robot effectors, will actually plan and act in the real world like an agent.

works.title: LaMDA
works.why: Cited as an example of a large language model developer letting the model query arbitrary URLs, illustrating tool-to-agent slippage.

works.title: Adept
works.why: Cited alongside LaMDA as an example of large model developers granting models risky real-world access.

works.title: An Introduction to Wittgenstein's Tractatus
works.why: Source of the anecdote about heliocentrism feeling counterintuitive, used as an analogy for why treating GPT-3 as agent-like feels unnatural yet is correct.

works.title: Story of Your Life
works.why: Cited as a fictional illustration of the variational/teleological way of describing a system's behavior, used to explain emergent agency.
